title: No Escape, Then a Rebuilding
overview: Amos ends his book with a final vision of judgment on the northern kingdom of Israel that no one can escape, followed by a promise that God will one day rebuild David's kingdom and bring the people home.

parts.label: The Lord at the altar (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Amos sees the Lord at an altar, most likely at Bethel, Israel's main shrine, ordering the building to collapse on the worshippers. Digging down to the grave, climbing to the sky, hiding on Mount Carmel or at the bottom of the sea all make one point: there is no hiding place from this judgment.

parts.label: The power behind the threat (vv. 5-6)
parts.note: This short hymn shows that the one making the threat can carry it out, since he touches the earth and it melts and he rules sky, land and sea. The land rising and sinking like the Nile pictures the whole country heaving like a river in its yearly flood.

parts.label: Israel is not untouchable (vv. 7-8)
parts.note: God says Israel is no more special to him than the distant Cushites, south of Egypt, and that he also guided the Philistines from Caphtor (probably Crete) and the Arameans from Kir. Being rescued from Egypt long ago does not protect Israel now, though God adds that he will not wipe out Jacob's descendants completely.

parts.label: The sieve (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: Israel will be shaken among the nations like grain in a sieve, and those who boast that disaster cannot reach them will die. Scholars are unsure of the image's exact sense: it may mean no guilty person slips through, or that the good grain is kept while the rest is lost.

parts.label: David's fallen shelter (vv. 11-12)
parts.note: David's royal house is pictured as a collapsed booth that God will repair and restore to its old size, ruling again over Edom, a hostile neighbor, and other nations. Many scholars think this hopeful ending was added after Jerusalem fell, and Christians read it in light of Jesus because the book of Acts quotes it when welcoming non-Jews.

parts.label: Harvests and homecoming (vv. 13-15)
parts.note: The harvest will be so huge that the plowing for next season catches up with the reapers still gathering this one. The people will return from exile, rebuild their towns, and be planted in their land for good, reversing the losses threatened earlier in the book.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the closing promises of rebuilding and return are fulfilled spiritually in the church welcoming all nations or still point to a future literal restoration of the Jewish people in their land, and both sides appeal to the way the book of Acts quotes this passage.
think: When a group believes it has been specially chosen or favored, what keeps that belief from turning into a feeling that nothing bad can ever happen to it?
